subject: Spec: Add finer grained read restrictions as part of loadTable (#13879)
body:
Add an optional read-restrictions field to LoadTableResult so a catalog
can return the result of evaluating fine grained access policies for the
calling user. The restrictions are enforced by the client, which
requires a trust relationship between the engine and the catalog; how
that trust is established is out of scope for this change.

ReadRestrictions carries two optional fields:

- required-column-projections: a list of Action objects, each naming a
  column by field-id along with the transformation to apply. Action uses
  a discriminator on the action property, with mask-alphanum,
  mask-to-fixed-value, replace-with-null, show-first-4, show-last-4,
  truncate-to-year, truncate-to-month, sha-256-global and
  sha-256-query-local defined. Each action produces a value of the same
  type as the input column.

- required-row-filter: an Expression evaluated against original,
  untransformed column values. Projections are applied to the rows that
  survive the filter.

Enforcement is fail-closed. A reader that supports read restrictions
must fail any read it cannot satisfy in full, including unrecognized
action or expression types and actions that cannot be loaded, parsed, or
evaluated, and must not silently return raw, partial, or empty results.
The restrictions apply to every read performed with a given response,
including subsequent planTableScan and fetchScanTasks calls, and may
differ between requests or between authentication scopes. A missing or
empty ReadRestrictions object imposes no restrictions.

Approved on the dev list with 8 binding +1 votes and no -1 votes:
https://lists.apache.org/thread/0zloqhp8wkgyn04yg69j71cwcg5n7g74

subject: Spark: Reject `rewrite_table_path` for encrypted tables (#17988)
body:
For an encrypted source table the rewrite completes and produces a target that
cannot be read. RewriteTablePathUtil resolves an EncryptionManager from the
FileIO and ManifestListWriter mints a fresh data encryption key for the staged
manifest list, but rewriteManifestList declares the writer as a bare
FileAppender and never calls toManifestListFile(), which is the sole caller of
addManifestListKeyMetadata. Meanwhile the rewrite copies the source table's
encryption-keys list and the snapshot key-id verbatim, so the target's manifest
lists are encrypted under a key that is registered nowhere. The copied manifests
are separately written through the plaintext ManifestFiles.write overloads.

Reject encrypted tables in validateInputs() instead. The guard tests
table.io() instanceof EncryptingFileIO, which is the same expression
RewriteTablePathUtil branches on when it resolves the encryption manager, so the
guard cannot fail open against this defect.

subject: Core, AWS: Fix case-insensitive handling of REST response header field names (#17979)
body:
* Core: Read REST response headers without regard to case

Freshness-aware table loading did nothing when the catalog server wrote the
ETag response header in any spelling other than ETag. HTTPClient collected
response headers into a map keyed by the name exactly as received and
RESTSessionCatalog copied that into another HashMap and read the tag back as
HttpHeaders.ETAG, so a server sending etag left the table cache empty, no
later load sent If-None-Match, and nothing surfaced that the server had
answered with a tag.

Header field names are case-insensitive (RFC 9110) and lowercase is mandatory
in HTTP/2 (RFC 9113), so the spelling a server chose cannot decide whether a
client finds the header. Both maps are now case-insensitive.

* AWS: Read the S3 signer's Cache-Control response header without regard to case

canBeCached looked Cache-Control up in a plain HashMap filled with the
server's own spelling, so a server writing cache-control never had its sign
responses cached and every S3 request signed remotely again.

* Ground the header-case comments in RFC 9110 alone

Mentioning HTTP/2's mandatory lowercase alongside the rule read as if the
change were about HTTP/2 conformance. The rule is RFC 9110 case-insensitivity;
HTTP/2 only explains why some servers emit lowercase, which belongs with the
test fixtures that simulate them. Also drops a comment that got duplicated.

subject: Core: Retry requests with an Idempotency-Key on retriable errors (#17947)
body:
* Core: Retry requests with an Idempotency-Key on retriable errors

ExponentialHttpRequestRetryStrategy only applied the idempotent retriable
status codes (408, 500, 502, 503, 504) when the HTTP method itself was
idempotent. Mutation endpoints are POST, so a request that already carries
an Idempotency-Key header - which the server guarantees is safe to replay -
was not retried on 502/504 or on 503 without a Retry-After header.

Treat a request carrying the Idempotency-Key header as retry-safe for these
codes, in both the response and network-exception retry paths. Requests
without the header keep the previous conservative behavior.

* Core: Address review feedback on idempotency-key retries

- Update testIdempotentCreateReplayAfterSimulated503: the client now
  auto-retries a keyed POST on 503 and the server replays the finalized
  200, so the call succeeds transparently. Assert success directly
  instead of expecting a thrown 503 followed by a manual retry.
- Add testIdempotentCreateRetryCarriesSameKey pinning the invariant that
  every transport attempt of a retried keyed POST carries the identical
  Idempotency-Key.
- Clarify the retry-safety comment in ExponentialHttpRequestRetryStrategy
  (idempotent method OR Idempotency-Key header), which no longer means
  strict HTTP idempotency.

* Core: Address review nits on idempotency-key retry test

- Import CopyOnWriteArrayList instead of using its fully-qualified name.
- Drop the redundant equality assertion in testIdempotentCreateRetryCarriesSameKey;
  the filter already guarantees equality, so hasSize(2) is the real guard.

subject: Core, Hive, Spark: Auto close JsonGenerator using try-with-resources (#17931)
body:
* Core, Hive, Spark: Close JsonGenerator instead of only flushing it

Ten sites created a JsonGenerator, called flush(), and left it unclosed.
flush() pushes buffered content to the target and flushes the target itself,
so the output was correct, but only close() returns the generator's char
buffers to the thread's BufferRecycler (_releaseBuffers) and returns the
recycler to the pool (IOContext.close). Without it, every serialization
allocates a fresh char[4000] concat buffer instead of reusing one.

Each generator now joins its enclosing try-with-resources so it closes
before its target. The explicit flush() remains only where a value is read
off the target inside the try: JsonUtil.generate and
TableMetadataParser.toJson read StringWriter.toString(), and
HMSTablePropertyHelper.hashOf reads HashWriter.getHash(). The last is
ordering-sensitive, since AUTO_CLOSE_TARGET makes closing the generator
close the HashWriter, and a closed HashWriter rejects getHash().

A JMH benchmark over TableMetadataParser measured a fixed 8,016 B/op
allocation reduction independent of document size, which is one char[4000]
plus its object header. For a ~1 KB document that is 10,616 -> 2,600 B/op
and 0.860 -> 0.730 us/op; for ~41 KB it is 49,680 -> 41,664 B/op.

On a failure mid-serialization, close() now auto-completes open contexts
(AUTO_CLOSE_JSON_CONTENT) and flushes partial content, where the flush()
was previously skipped. The resulting metadata file is orphaned either way
because the commit fails.

* Restore explicit generator.flush() calls

Review feedback: relying on close() to flush is correct but implicit, and it
contradicts JsonUtil.generate, which was cited as the pattern this change
follows and which does call flush().

Restoring the calls keeps this change to a single concern: adding the
generator to the enclosing try-with-resources so it is closed. The
buffer-recycling win comes entirely from close() releasing the char buffer
to the BufferRecycler, not from dropping the flush, so nothing measured is
lost. The flush is now redundant with close() at these sites, which costs
one extra flush() on the underlying stream per write.

subject: Parquet: Decode ENUM/JSON columns as UTF-8 in row-group filter conversions (#17157)
body:
* Parquet: Decode ENUM/JSON columns as UTF-8 in row-group filter conversions

ParquetConversions.converterFromParquet special-cased only the UTF8 original
type, so for ENUM- or JSON-annotated Parquet columns it fell through to the
binary path and returned a ByteBuffer. Iceberg maps both ENUM and JSON to
StringType (MessageTypeToType), so at read time the metrics/dictionary row-group
filters compared that ByteBuffer against a CharSequence predicate literal and
threw:

  class java.nio.HeapByteBuffer cannot be cast to class java.lang.CharSequence

This is reachable for files written by other engines (e.g. Flink, which uses
JSON columns) and added via add_files: querying such a column with a predicate
triggers row-group filtering. Treat ENUM and JSON like UTF8 and decode them to a
CharSequence. The import/metrics path (ParquetConversions.convertValue) already
switches on the Iceberg type and was unaffected.
